title: Polymorphism and Virtual Functions
relevance: Interviewers use virtual functions, override bugs, vtables, and object slicing to test whether candidates understand how C++ dynamic polymorphism actually works.

phases.goal: Establish compile-time vs run-time polymorphism, upcasting, static binding, and what virtual/override/final mean.

must_hit.point: C++ supports compile-time polymorphism (function overloading, templates) and run-time polymorphism via inheritance and virtual functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both kinds and ties run-time polymorphism to virtual functions and inheritance.

must_hit.point: Upcasting is safe: a base pointer or reference may point to a derived object because a derived object is a base object.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States base pointer/reference to derived is valid and explains the is-a relationship.

must_hit.point: Without virtual, C++ uses static binding: the call is wired from the pointer type at compile time, so a Car* to AdvancedCar still runs Car::startEngine.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains early binding from pointer type and gives the non-virtual Car/AdvancedCar outcome.

must_hit.point: Marking the base function virtual enables dynamic dispatch so the call uses the actual object type; override forces a true override and final blocks further overriding or inheritance.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions virtual for late binding, override as a compile-time signature check, and final to seal a function or class.

probes: What is the difference between compile-time and run-time polymorphism in C++?
What happens if you call startEngine through a Car* that points to AdvancedCar when startEngine is not virtual?

hints.1: Think about when the call target is chosen: compile time or run time.
hints.2: Contrast function overloading/templates with inheritance plus virtual, then describe upcasting without virtual.
hints.3: Compile-time: overloading and templates; run-time: virtual. Non-virtual Car* calls Car::startEngine even if the object is AdvancedCar.

phases.goal: Explain how dynamic dispatch is implemented with vtables and vptrs, and how to force a static base call.

must_hit.point: A class with at least one virtual function gets a per-class vtable (static array of function pointers to the most-derived accessible virtuals) and each object gets a hidden vptr to that table.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says one vtable per class, one vptr per object, and that the vtable holds the addresses used for dispatch.

must_hit.point: A virtual call through a base pointer reads the object's vptr, indexes the vtable, and jumps to the function; that indirection is slightly slower and usually prevents inlining.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the indirect lookup path and names both per-call cost and lost inlining.

must_hit.point: Qualifying with Base:: (for example Car::startEngine()) bypasses dynamic dispatch and statically calls that base version.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows scope resolution to invoke the base implementation from an override.

probes: How does dynamic dispatch work under the hood?
How can a derived override still call the base version of a virtual function?

hints.1: Picture each polymorphic object carrying a pointer to a shared function table for its class.
hints.2: Name vtable versus vptr, then walk a virtual call: vptr → table slot → function.
hints.3: vtable is one static table per class; vptr is embedded per object; Base::func() forces a static call.

phases.goal: Contrast C++’s opt-in virtual model and polymorphic usage via pointers/references versus value semantics.

must_hit.point: Unlike Python where methods are virtual by default, C++ defaults to static binding for performance and requires an explicit virtual for dynamic dispatch.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares Python’s default virtual methods with C++ requiring virtual to pay the dispatch cost only when needed.

must_hit.point: Polymorphism only works through pointers or references; copying by value slices the derived part and breaks dynamic behavior.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States pass/assign by Base value slices, and that Base* or Base& preserve the dynamic type.

probes: Why does C++ make you write virtual instead of making all methods virtual by default?
Why must polymorphic objects be passed by pointer or reference?

hints.1: Connect the language default to performance and to how objects are passed.
hints.2: Static binding avoids vptr/indirection until you opt in; value copies only keep the base subobject.
hints.3: C++ prioritises performance so virtual is explicit; by-value assignment invokes the Base copy and sets the new object’s vptr to the Base vtable.

phases.goal: Apply override rules and catch classic traps: hiding, default arguments, and object slicing.

must_hit.point: Override requires an exact signature match including const-ness; a same-name different-signature derived function hides the base and is not an override.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the missing-const display example: derived display(int) hides Base::display(int) const.

must_hit.point: Virtual functions dispatch dynamically, but default arguments are bound statically from the static pointer type—so Base* p to Derived calling print() runs Derived::print with Base’s default 10, not Derived’s 20.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States output Derived: 10 and explains static default vs dynamic function choice.

must_hit.point: Passing AdvancedCar by value into a Car parameter slices away derived state (for example batteryLevel) and identify() runs as the base Car version.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes by-value printByValue slicing and output I am a standard Car.

probes: Spot the bug: derived display(int) versus base display(int) const—what happens and how do you prevent it?
What does Base* p = new Derived(); p->print(); print if both declare defaults 10 and 20?
What happens if you pass a derived object to a function that takes the base by value?

hints.1: Check signature match, default-argument binding, and whether the parameter is a value or a pointer/reference.
hints.2: Missing const → hiding; defaults follow the pointer type; by-value copy keeps only the Base subobject.
hints.3: Use override to catch mismatches; expect Derived: 10; slicing drops derived members and the copy’s vptr points at the Base vtable.

tradeoffs.topic: Static binding (default) vs virtual dynamic dispatch
tradeoffs.strong_answer: C++ defaults to static binding for performance; virtual adds a per-object vptr and a slower indirect call that usually cannot be inlined, so you opt in only when run-time polymorphism is needed.

tradeoffs.topic: Polymorphic objects by value vs by pointer/reference
tradeoffs.strong_answer: By-value copy/assignment slices to the Base subobject, resets the vptr to the Base vtable, and loses derived state; Base* or Base& preserve dynamic type and correct virtual dispatch.

tradeoffs.topic: Python virtual-by-default vs C++ explicit virtual
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Python methods are virtual by default so a base reference always hits a derived override if present; C++ requires writing virtual because it prioritises performance.

gotchas.trap: A derived function with the same name but different parameters (or missing const) looks like an override but hides the base function instead.
gotchas.correction: Override needs an exact signature match including const-ness; use the override specifier so mismatches become compile errors.

gotchas.trap: Assuming default arguments on a virtual function come from the dynamic type.
gotchas.correction: The function is chosen dynamically, but defaults are substituted statically from the pointer/reference type—Base* yields Base’s default (10) even when Derived::print runs.

gotchas.trap: Passing or assigning a derived object to a base object by value and expecting polymorphism.
gotchas.correction: That slices: only the Base subobject is copied, derived data is lost, and virtual calls resolve as Base; pass Base* or Base& instead.

gotchas.trap: Calling a derived-only method like activateAutopilot through a Car* after upcasting.
gotchas.correction: The base pointer only exposes the base interface; derived-only members are not visible without a different mechanism, and non-virtual base methods still bind statically to the base version.
